tutorial_example_entry.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: State the value-based definition of the unit step function and interpret it as the basic continuous-time on-off signal used to build shifted, delayed, and rectangular-pulse signal descriptions.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Introduction to Definition of the Unit Step Function

blocks.text: Introduce the unit step as the continuous-time switch function. In this lesson, we use it to indicate which time side of the axis is active and which side is off.
Teach the rule for times before the switch: for $t<0$, the switch is off, so $u(t)=0$.
Teach the rule for times after the switch: for $t>0$, the switch is on, so $u(t)=1$.
Use one base case to show both sides: if $t=-1$, then $u(-1)=0$, and if $t=2$, then $u(2)=1$.
Set the course convention at the boundary by declaring $u(0)=1$ for this topic line and using that same convention everywhere in this module.
This definition is the core building block for shifted and delayed step functions, and later it will be used to construct rectangular pulses and other on-off signal forms.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Evaluating the Unit Step Before and After the Switch

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate $u(-4)$ and $u(3)$ with the definition from the tutorial.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the unit-step rule as the guide: for $t<0$, the signal is off and $u(t)=0$, and for $t>0$, the signal is on and $u(t)=1$.
Classify the first query: $-4<0$, so it is on the left side of the switch.
Apply the left-side rule to the query and report the result: $u(-4)=0$.
Classify the second query: $3>0$, so it is on the right side of the switch.
Apply the right-side rule and report the result: $u(3)=1$.
Final answer: $u(-4)=0$, $u(3)=1$. In this lesson format, any non-boundary point is solved by that same two-step pointwise classification and substitution pattern.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Evaluating the Unit Step at the Switching Time

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate $u(0)$ and decide whether it differs from both one-sided limits.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same switch rule as the earlier sections: for $t<0$, $u(t)=0$, and for $t>0$, $u(t)=1$. The new cue here is to handle the boundary-time case.
Recognize $t=0$ is not a strict interior point, so it is not covered by either the left-hand or right-hand branch alone.
Apply the lesson convention directly at the boundary: $u(0)=1$ for this topic line.
For contrast, the neighbor values are $u(0^-)=0$ and $u(0^+)=1$ under the previously learned rules.
Result: the boundary point is $u(0)=1$, which does differ from the left-limit value at zero and matches the chosen on-value convention used in this lesson.

sections.section_title: Reading the Unit Step Function from a Time-Axis Graph

image_slots.image_description: A time-axis graph of a binary unit-step function showing a constant 0 level for left-side times and a constant 1 level for right-side times, with a single jump at a marked switching instant. Include clear axis labels, horizontal segments only, and a visible switch marker.

example_content.example_prompt: Read the graph and compute $u(t)$ for three selected times, including the switch instant.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the graph as the cue: identify the switching instant first, then read which side of the jump each query time is on.
If the switch is at $t=0$, then the left-side region is $t<0$ and the right-side region is $t>0$.
Classify the selected times: $t=-2$ lies left of the switch, so $u(-2)=0$.
For the switch instant $t=0$, apply the lesson convention, so $u(0)=1$. In this lesson that is the same boundary convention used in symbolic work.
For $t=2$, the time is right of the jump, so $u(2)=1$. Therefore the on interval is $t\ge 0$ and the off interval is $t<0$ under this convention.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Recognizing the Unit Step as the Basic Continuous-Time Switching Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite and interpret the piecewise signal defined by $x(t)u(t)$ with $x(t)=t^2$.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the cue that multiplication by $u(t)$ gates the signal by time region, so $x(t)u(t)$ must be split by the same $u(t)$ regions.
From the learned rule, if $t<0$, then $u(t)=0$, so $x(t)u(t)=t^2\cdot 0=0$ on the off region.
For $t>0$, the on region has $u(t)=1$, so $x(t)u(t)=t^2\cdot 1=t^2$ there.
Using the lesson convention at the boundary, $u(0)=1$, so $x(0)u(0)=0^2\cdot 1=0$ and the boundary aligns with the right-side expression.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Unit Step Before and After the Switch

prompt_blocks.text: Evaluate $u(-0.1)$ and $u(8)$ with the definition from the tutorial.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $-0.1<0$, the unit step is off there, so $u(-0.1)=0$. Because $8>0$, the unit step is on there, so $u(8)=1$.

prompt_blocks.text: Evaluate $u(10)$ and $u(-7)$ with the definition from the tutorial.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $10>0$, the unit step is on there, so $u(10)=1$. Because $-7<0$, the unit step is off there, so $u(-7)=0$.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Evaluating the Unit Step at the Switching Time

prompt_blocks.text: Under this lesson convention, what are the values of $u(-0.01)$, $u(0)$, and $u(0.01)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Negative time is off, so $u(-0.01)=0$. The lesson convention sets the switching time to the on value, so $u(0)=1$. Positive time is also on, so $u(0.01)=1$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which statement correctly describes the boundary-time value under this lesson convention?

choice_blocks.text: $u(0)=1$, so it matches $u(0.01)$ and differs from $u(-0.01)$
$u(0)=0$, so it matches $u(-0.01)$ and differs from $u(0.01)$
$u(0)=\frac{1}{2}$, so it sits halfway between the left and right values
$u(0)=1$, so it matches $u(-0.01)$ and differs from $u(0.01)$
$u(0)=0$, so both nearby values are also $0$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The lesson convention assigns the switch instant to the on value, so $u(0)=1$. The nearby positive time $0.01$ is also on, while the nearby negative time $-0.01$ is off.

image_slots.image_description: A minimal time-axis graph of a unit step with a single jump at $t=0$. The graph is 0 for $t<0 and 1 for t\ge0$. Include clear axis labels and a visible switch marker at 0.
A minimal time-axis graph of a unit step with a single jump at $t=2$. The graph is 0 for $t<2 and 1 for t\ge2$. Include clear axis labels and a visible switch marker at 2.

prompt_blocks.text: From the graph, identify $u(-3)$, $u(0)$, and the interval where the signal is on.

choice_blocks.text: $u(-3)=0$, $u(0)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\ge 0$.
$u(-3)=1$, $u(0)=1$, and the signal is on for $t<0$.
$u(-3)=0$, $u(0)=0$, and the signal is on for $t>0$.
$u(-3)=0$, $u(0)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\le 0$.
$u(-3)=0.5$, $u(0)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\ge 0$.

questions.correct_answer: $u(-3)=0$, $u(0)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\ge 0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The graph switches at $t=0$, so $t=-3$ is left of the jump and gives $0$. At the switching time, the lesson convention gives $u(0)=1$.
Therefore the signal is on for $t\ge 0$, which matches choice A.

prompt_blocks.text: From the graph, identify $u(1)$, $u(2)$, and the interval where the signal is on.

choice_blocks.text: $u(1)=0$, $u(2)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\ge 2$.
$u(1)=1$, $u(2)=1$, and the signal is on for $t<2$.
$u(1)=0$, $u(2)=0$, and the signal is on for $t>2$.
$u(1)=0$, $u(2)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\ge 0$.
$u(1)=0.5$, $u(2)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\le 2$.

questions.correct_answer: $u(1)=0$, $u(2)=1$, and the signal is on for $t\ge 2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The graph switches at $t=2$, so $t=1$ is left of the jump and gives $0$. At the switching time, the lesson convention gives $u(2)=1$.
Therefore the signal is on for $t\ge 2$, which matches choice A.

sections.section_title: Recognizing the Unit Step as the Basic Continuous-Time Switching Signal

choice_blocks.text: It shifts the signal in phase instead of turning it on and off in time.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The unit step is the right-side gate: $u(t)=0$ for $t<0$ and $u(t)=1$ for $t\ge0$ under the lesson convention. So multiplying by $u(t)$ kills the left side and leaves $t^2$ unchanged on the right side.

choice_blocks.text: It changes the signal's phase instead of gating its amplitude.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The same gate applies here: $u(t)$ is off for $t<0$ and on for $t\ge0$. So the product suppresses $3t-1$ on the left side and passes it through unchanged on the right side.
